docs.title: JElib
docs.text:
JElib is a growing collection of Houdini tools designed to remove friction from your workflow, so you can stay focused on creating.

At its core is the JE Asset Browser, an easy way to organize, browse, and access the assets you already have. Build your own reusable libraries of models, materials, setups, and other assets, then quickly find and bring them into your projects without digging through folders or rebuilding things you've already made. It supports Karma, Redshift and Octane.

docs.title: JE Asset Browser
docs.text:
Add any folder of assets (textures, materials, HDRIs, and geometry) and drag them into your scene. It works in both the OBJ and LOP (Solaris) contexts.

Install JElib, then point it at your assets.

docs.title: Additional Tools
docs.text:
The paid version of JElib comes with additional addons and tooling, with more to be added over time.

  • Collect Files — copy a scene's external files into one folder, with a self-contained hip beside them, ready to archive or hand off.
  • Relink Files — find broken file references across your scene and repath them, including inside USD layers.
Collect FilesGather a scene into one portable folder. Relink FilesRepath missing references.

docs.title: Animation & sequences
docs.text: JElib handles three kinds of moving asset: frame sequences on disk, a single animated Alembic, and a rigged/animated FBX. Each is detected during the scan and imported as an animated setup: no manual $F wiring, no KineFX chain to build by hand.

docs.title: What gets detected
docs.text:
On disk Card badge Asset Info Numbered frame files: smoke_0001.vdb, anim.0001.abc, cache_v1.0001.bgeo.sc SEQ (a VDB sequence badges VDB) Frames row, e.g. 1-120 One .abc holding animation ABC — .fbx with a skin binding and animation curves ANIM — .fbx with a skin binding but no animation RIG —

Rigged FBX detection reads the file's own skin/animation markers, so it works on binary and ASCII FBX alike.

Detected frame sequences collapse into one card with a $F template. Two or more numbered files sharing a stem in the same folder make a family; LOD siblings (crate_lod0/1/2) are excluded. Sequence Detection under Browser Display lets you keep numbered files separate or group them as sequences, with an override on a folder's right-click menu.

docs.title: Frame sequences
docs.text:
Supported for .abc, .bgeo / .bgeo.sc, .vdb, and .rs. See Supported file formats.

  • OBJ / SOP — the import reads the $F template, so the asset plays with the timeline as you scrub.
  • Solaris — the same, and the Bake .usd / Auto modes write a time-sampled USD over the sequence's frame range instead of freezing frame 1. A baked sequence cache is only rebuilt when its frames or range actually change.
  • VDB sequences drive the volume LOP's time-dependent sampling and get a volume shader for your renderer.
  • Missing frames are allowed but flagged in the import notes: the instancing retime below assumes a contiguous cache and copies pop where a frame is absent.
  • A $F sequence baked to USD authors no proxy or collision (simproxy) representation; those are static-asset-only. The render mesh bakes as usual.

$F sequences appear in Houdini's native Solaris Asset Catalog / Paint Instances gallery alongside rigged FBX (VDB and .rs proxy sequences don't; see Houdini's native galleries).

docs.title: Rigged & animated FBX
docs.text:
Drop one and JElib builds a KineFX character chain rather than a plain file SOP: fbxcharacterimport feeding a MotionClip pack → cycle → eval into a bonedeform, so the character actually deforms on the timeline. Rigged FBX default to import scale 1.0 (not the static-FBX 0.01).

In Solaris, the LOP Import combo swaps its two build modes for skeleton-aware ones:

Mode What you get USD Skel The live, editable graph in the stage: KineFX SOPs in a self-contained sopcreate host feeding a sopcharacterimport LOP Bake USD A real UsdSkel component on disk: SkelRoot / Skeleton / SkelAnimation, plus a proxy representation and the material under the component Use Cached USD References whatever cache exists; never re-bakes

Baked skeletons carry their materials, including textures from a Mixamo-style <name>.fbm sidecar folder that ordinary name-grouping can't associate.

Native frame placement

A clip bakes exactly where it sits in its own timeline: no loop, no normalize. USD holds the last sample past the end of the range, so the character freezes on its final pose rather than snapping back once the clip plays through. Looping is a separate, composition-time choice. See below.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
A Loop checkbox appears in the preview panel's Import Settings for any asset whose bake carries animation: a rigged/animated FBX or an $F sequence. VDB sequences and .rs proxy sequences don't get it; they don't bake through the same clip mechanism. Off (the default), the animation plays once and holds on its last frame; on, it repeats for the whole scene playback range.

Loop works in every Solaris import mode, live or baked, and for rigged FBX in the OBJ/SOP context too. JElib picks whichever mechanism the mode can actually carry:

Mode Mechanism Baked / referenced USD (Bake USD, Auto when it can write) A USD Value Clip wrapping the one-cycle cache, authored at drop time against the scene's playback range Rigged FBX, live (SOP Create, OBJ, USD Skel) The KineFX MotionClip cycle's Cycles After, sized to the playback range $F sequence, live (SOP Create, Component Builder) A Timeshift SOP that wraps instead of clamping to the last frame

A $F sequence imported into an OBJ/SOP network is the one case Loop doesn't reach. That chain reads the frame straight off the scene, so it neither loops nor holds past the sequence's own range. Import it into Solaris to loop it.

Whichever applies, the node it builds is an ordinary part of the network: you can flip its loop toggle by hand afterwards if the scene's playback range changes.

docs.title: Per-instance time offset
docs.text:
With Create Instances on an animated asset, every copy would otherwise play the same frame at the same time. The generated time-offset wrangle staggers them: a field of flowers that don't all bloom on the same frame.

In OBJ/SOP imports, the controls sit on that wrangle's parameters, next to the distribution and wind controls:

Parameter What it does Start Frame The sequence frame every copy starts on before its offset; raise it to skip preroll. Playback anchors to the scene's playback start, so the result reads the same on any timeline. Spread Mode Random (seeded per copy) · Step (ramped by copy index, a wave) · Attribute (frame driven directly by a point attribute) Spread Maximum frames of stagger across copies. 0 = no stagger. Loop Wrap the animation so copies stay spread across the whole range at every frame. Off: each copy plays once and holds on its last frame. Seed Random mode only. Offset Remap Step mode only: reshapes the linear index ramp that scales the offset. Offset Attribute Attribute mode only: the 0–1 point attribute to scale the offset by (default factor). A missing attribute reads as 0, i.e. same timing for every copy.

How each source is retimed — each format is retimed differently, and some combinations aren't offered:

Source Mechanism Notes Single animated .abc Per-copy Alembic time on packed prims The viewport can't draw per-copy Alembic time; it renders correctly. An archive whose content doesn't actually move is treated as static, even if it carries a time range .bgeo / .bgeo.sc sequence Bare points, each loading its own frame file Karma and Redshift honour the per-point material; Octane uses the object material .rs proxy sequence Same, via the proxy file per point Redshift only .abc sequence — Create Instances is unavailable. Every offset copy needs its own archive open, which is unusably slow. Bake to .bgeo.sc and instance that instead. Solaris / USD A Cache LOP + Retime Instances, with bucketed per-instance offsets Automatic: no separate offset controls in the preview panel. Scattered copies each play the animation at their own phase, on a native USD PointInstancer. See Per-instance time offset in the stage.

OBJ/SOP timing controls

The parameters above are shared by OBJ/SOP imports of a .abc prop and a .bgeo.sc cache. Solaris setups have their own Random, Step, Noise, and Custom modes; see Instancing in the stage.

docs.title: Adding your libraries
docs.text:
On first launch, JElib asks where your assets are located. Choose a folder on your local or external drive, and it lists the libraries inside it. Tick the ones you want, then press Add Libraries.

JElib also detects assets you keep in the cloud: Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud Drive and Synology Drive. Assets on a server or NAS are covered too, through on-demand caching: JElib pulls them into a local cache as you use them. See Remote & cloud libraries.

docs.title: Add another library
docs.text:
If your assets live in different locations, you can also add libraries manually in the Libraries tab. There are three ways:

  • Click Add… at the bottom left.
  • Drag a folder in from Explorer/Finder.
  • Right-click empty space in the table → Add Library….

Any path works, not just the one you picked at first-run.

To re-open the first-run setup itself, use Libraries → Re-run setup…; it's additive, and never removes or rewrites the libraries you already have. See the Libraries tab reference.

docs.title: Scene-local assets ($HIP/tex and $HIP/geo)
docs.text:
Working on a shot or project where textures or geometry live next to the scene file? Tick Show Local Library ($HIP) in the Libraries tab footer: JElib surfaces a Local Library in the navigation tree if a tex or geo folder sits beside the saved .hip. Imports from it keep portable $HIP/tex/… or $HIP/geo/… paths, so the scene and its assets travel together.

See Libraries tab reference for the full behaviour.

docs.title: Portable paths (Asset Variable)
docs.text:
First-run setup stores your library paths relative to an Asset Variable, so the same config can resolve to a different folder on each machine. Expand Asset Variable to pick an existing Houdini variable or name another managed one, and Resolved Folder shows where it points here. Libraries outside it keep absolute paths.

Using one config across several machines is covered in Remote & cloud libraries.

docs.title: Texture atlases
docs.text: A texture atlas is one image holding many small pieces: foliage leaf cards, decals, ground debris, trim sheets. Import one and JElib traces each packed piece into its own card on a generated grid, ready to scatter.

docs.title: Importing an atlas
docs.text:
Atlas assets from Quixel and Fab are detected automatically. Drop one in and JElib routes it through the Atlas Splitter, which reads the atlas's opacity and colour maps and traces each packed piece into its own card on a generated grid, instead of a single flat quad.

Have a loose texture you know is an atlas? Select it and tick Import as Atlas in the preview panel:

Splits the packed pieces in this texture into individual cards on a grid. Requires the Atlas Splitter HDA.

It's an explicit opt-in (off by default), shown for loose textures.

This source atlas contains six leaf shapes:

The splitter produces separate pieces. Here, Enable Layout spreads them out for inspection, Divide triangulates the shapes, and viewport materials and textures are hidden so the geometry is easy to see.

Needs the Atlas Splitter HDA

Splitting relies on the JE_Atlas_Splitter HDA. If it isn't installed, the atlas loads onto a plain flat grid with no piece splitting, and if you asked for instances, JElib warns you that the whole grid will be copied.

docs.title: Scatter the cards
docs.text:
With instancing, each traced piece becomes a variant: turning on Create Instances scatters the cards across your points with per-card scale, rotation, and tilt. Atlases always scatter with Copy to Points; the Instance method picker covers models and plants.

Set Source Up to +Z for cards

Card geometry usually faces +Z (the card normal), but the instancing Source Up control defaults to +Y (upright models/plants). Switch it to +Z so scattered cards orient correctly. Turn off the "long axis → X" rotation for non-foliage atlases like decals or pebbles.

docs.title: Typical uses
docs.text: Foliage leaf cards for trees and bushes, scattered decals and ground debris, trim and pebble sheets, anything shipped as many small pieces packed into one texture.

docs.title: Free and Paid editions
docs.text:
Both editions include JE Asset Browser with Karma, Redshift and Octane support. You supply your own assets; JElib helps you browse and import them.

Free Paid JE Asset Browser Up to 1,000 assets No asset limit Relink Files Not included Included Collect Files Not included Included

docs.title: The Free asset limit
docs.text: The 1,000-asset limit applies across your libraries, not separately to each folder. Assets beyond the limit remain visible as locked cards and cannot be imported. Your files are not deleted or changed when the limit is reached.

docs.title: Switching editions
docs.text: Run the Paid edition's installer over your existing installation, then restart Houdini. Your libraries, favorites and cache are kept. See Updating for installation and edition-change instructions.

docs.title: Find & organize
docs.text:
However big your library gets, four tools get you to the right asset fast: search, filter, favorites, and browse.

Everything starts in the navigation tree on the left. It mirrors your libraries and their folders, and whatever you select there sets the current view: the scope that search, filters and favorites work within. Pick a library to see all of it, or a folder to narrow in. See the Browse tab reference for its nodes and right-click actions.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Type in the Search assets… field in the toolbar. It filters live as you type, matching asset names and tags in the current view. An active search keeps a highlighted border when you leave the field. If nothing matches, use Clear search to remove the search term while keeping your other filters.

  1. Select a folder or library in the navigation tree.
  2. Type a name or tag into Search assets….
  3. Select a result to inspect it before loading it into your scene.

To search by tag, use the tag: keyword: everything before it is a name query, everything after is a comma-separated tag list.

You type You get concrete assets named concrete tag: gravel assets tagged gravel concrete tag: road, urban concrete assets tagged road or urban

The tag: keyword highlights as you type, and known tags auto-complete.

Two search fields

Search assets… filters assets in the library or folder you've selected. Search collections… searches across all your libraries and jumps to the collection you pick.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
Click Filter in the toolbar to open the filter panel. Toggles apply live; the button stays lit while any filter is active.

  1. Click Filter.
  2. Choose the asset type, format, renderer, or tag to narrow to the assets you'd like to browse.
Filter popup with Material selected

The Filter button shows the count (Filter · 1), and a chip row above the grid names each one, so it is always clear why the results are narrowed.

Material filter active: the Filter button counts it, and a chip row above the grid names it
  • Favorites — show only starred assets.
  • Asset Type — Material, HDRI, Model, Plant, Atlas, Texture, Node Tree.
  • Format — narrow models to one geometry format: FBX, OBJ, ABC, USD, BGEO, GLTF.
  • User Saved Materials — your own saved materials by renderer (Redshift, Octane, Karma) or USD Materials.
  • Tags — one toggle per tag present in the library.
  • Filter Range — flip All Libraries to widen search and filters to every library instead of just the current view. Clear all resets everything.

Click a chip to drop it, or Clear all to reset.

Same stem, several formats

Crate.fbx next to Crate.obj gives you one card per format. The first format present keeps the bare name, and the rest are suffixed (Crate (OBJ)). They share one thumbnail, and the Format filter narrows the grid to a single one.

docs.title: Favorites
docs.text:
Star the assets you reach for often and pull them up in one click.

  • Hover an asset and click the star at the top-right of its thumbnail. Favorited assets keep the star showing.
  • Right-click one or more selected assets → Add to Favorites / Remove from Favorites (the label counts your selection).

Once you star an asset, Favorites appears at the top of the navigation tree, so everything you've starred is one click away. Select it to show only those assets, and it goes away again when you remove the last one.

The star button in the toolbar (or Favorites in the filter panel) instead narrows your current view to starred assets; combine it with Browse or All Libraries to scope wide or narrow. Favorites persist across sessions.

docs.title: Browse your folders
docs.text:
By default the grid shows every asset under the folder you've selected in the navigation tree, sub-folders flattened into one view. That's great for scanning, less so for big trees.

Turn on Browse in the toolbar to walk the tree like Finder instead: the grid shows only this folder's contents. Sub-folders appear as tiles alongside the assets that live at this level.

  • Double-click a folder tile to enter it.
  • Double-click the .. tile at the top of the grid to go up one level. (It's hidden once you're at a library root.)
  • From the keyboard: Enter on a folder tile enters it, Backspace goes up one level, and the arrow keys move the selection.
  • The navigation tree stays in sync: select a folder there, or drill in the grid; either drives the other.

Browse off = search everything

Leave Browse off when you want search and filters to sweep the whole library at once. Turn it on when you know roughly where the asset lives and want to click your way there.

docs.title: Supported file formats
docs.text: JElib supports a wide range of asset types. This page covers what it recognises when it scans a library or receives a file, and what happens when you import each kind.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Extension What it is OBJ / SOP Solaris (LOP) Sequences .fbx Mesh, LODs, multi-piece kits, and rigged/animated characters file SOP (or split per piece); a KineFX chain when rigged Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD; a rigged FBX swaps the last two for USD Skel · Bake USD — .obj Mesh file SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD — .abc Alembic, which preserves the source hierarchy and per-piece names Dedicated alembic SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD Yes: $F frame families .bgeo / .bgeo.sc Houdini geometry file SOP Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD Yes: $F frame families .gltf / .glb glTF mesh (Sketchfab and similar downloads ship this) Dedicated import chain, LOD-aware Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD — .usd / .usdc / .usda / .usdz Already USD Referenced directly, no baking Referenced directly, no baking — .vdb OpenVDB volume file SOP + a volume shader for your renderer Native volume LOP Yes: $F frame families .rs Redshift Proxy redshift_packedProxySOP Native RS_Proxy LOP Yes: $F frame families

See Working in Solaris for what each LOP Import mode does, and Preferences → USD to set your default. Anything animated (a $F sequence, an animated Alembic, a rigged FBX) is covered on Animation & sequences.

VDB and RS Proxy carry their own shading

Both skip the generic material-building path. A VDB gets a dedicated volume shader per renderer (Karma/Redshift/Octane), and an RS Proxy carries its baked-in shading from export, so Create Material isn't offered for either.

.rs is also Redshift-only. Octane and Karma have no equivalent proxy format, so importing .rs with another renderer selected gives you an unshaded result until you switch to Redshift.

docs.title: Model materials
docs.text:
A model can bring its own materials. JElib reads the material slots the file declares (the .mtl beside an OBJ, the graph inside an FBX, the materials in a glTF), resolves the textures they point at, and builds one shader per slot instead of a single shader from the folder's texture set.

glTF needs Houdini 22

glTF and GLB take their materials on Houdini 22 only. On 20.5 and 21 they import as geometry with no material. A .glb that carries its textures inside the file also imports geometry-only; a .gltf with separate image files beside it is what JElib reads.

An FBX whose materials come from a <name>.fbm folder beside it keeps those — that sidecar is richer than the file's own graph. A rigged character reads its own material slots too, when the file's textures resolve.

A numeric value a file declares beside a texture — a base colour, metallic, roughness or opacity — is applied on top of the map, not replaced by it.

docs.title: Textures & PBR maps
docs.text: .jpg, .jpeg, .png, .tif, .tiff, .tx, .tga.

docs.title: Substance archives
docs.text:
.sbsar. Each archive shows up as one material card with an (SBSAR) suffix. The first time you import it, JElib bakes its maps with Houdini's built-in Substance support (no Labs or Adobe install needed) and builds the material from them like any texture set. Later imports reuse the baked maps.

Pick the size with Resolution: 4K, 2K, 1K or 512 (512 by default). Larger sizes take longer. Your pick carries over to the next archive until you restart Houdini. JElib bakes the archive's default settings, with normal maps in the OpenGL format every supported renderer reads.

To change the archive's settings in Houdini, turn on Use Substance SOP before you import. JElib then adds SideFX Labs' Substance Material node to the selected geometry instead of baking. Inside a geometry network, it goes after the node you have selected, or after the displayed node when nothing (or more than one node) is selected. The node holds the archive's controls and builds its own Principled Shader rather than a Redshift, Octane or Karma material. It needs SideFX Labs and works with geometry objects, not Solaris.

To swap the archive on a Substance Material node you already have, select the node and Shift-drag another archive into that network. The node loads the new archive and keeps its wiring and Size. Dropping the archive it already uses changes nothing, so your edits stay.

Houdini 24 removes the Substance node

Baking and Use Substance SOP both run on Houdini's Labs Substance Archive node, which SideFX will remove in Houdini 24.0. See the SideFX documentation.

docs.title: HDRIs
docs.text: .hdr, .hdri, and .exr. An .exr is only treated as an HDRI when its filename or the folder it sits in signals it (hdri, env, panorama, latlong, equirect, ibl, …), so HDRIs/sunset.exr counts. Otherwise it's read as a texture/render pass, since most .exr files aren't environment maps.

docs.title: Color palettes
docs.text: .ase, .gpl, .aco, .swatches, and a .txt whose name or contents look like a swatch list. See Color palettes.

docs.title: Node trees & saved materials
docs.text: Materials and node networks you save from Houdini live as .json inside the browser's own library folders. See Save to the browser. They aren't something you'd drop in from outside Houdini.

docs.title: Import into your scene
docs.text: Importing is the core move: JElib builds the nodes and wires the material for your renderer. If you just want the quick version, see Import your first asset. This page covers every way to import and every option along the way.

docs.title: Three ways to import
docs.text:
• Drag an asset from the grid into the network editor or the viewport. Ctrl/Shift-click several first to bring a multi-selection in together.
  • Double-click an asset, or select it and press Enter (loads every selected asset).
  • Select an asset and click Load into Scene in the preview panel.

Drop a model or plant on the 3D viewport and it lands where you released it: on the geometry surface under the cursor, else the ground plane, else the origin. This works in both the OBJ and Solaris (LOP-stage) contexts. A multi-drop fans the assets out side by side, and HDRIs become the active renderer's dome light. This applies to drags from the browser; OS file drops on the viewport keep Houdini's own behavior.

Drop a material onto an object to assign it

Drag a material onto geometry in the viewport and JElib builds it for your active renderer and assigns it to whatever is under the cursor, including bare primitive shapes and, in Solaris, USD prims. It targets the part under the cursor (a material slot / named part, or a GeomSubset in Solaris) and falls back to the whole object. Hold Ctrl to flip that for one drop. The whole drag-and-drop is a single undo step.

docs.title: Drag files in from outside Houdini
docs.text:
Drag a texture, PBR set, HDRI, or model straight from your OS file manager (Explorer/Finder) onto the network editor, and JElib imports it exactly like a browser drop: same nodes, same material for your active renderer, honouring your import settings (Force Absolute File Paths, Prefer 16-bit, Material Only…).

  • Drop a folder and JElib reads it as one asset: geometry + a PBR set becomes a model with its material built together; a textures-only folder becomes one material. LOD siblings (crate_lod0/1/2.fbx) collapse into a single model at your Default LOD (Preferences → Import); a folder holding only a _High source mesh imports that. Drop a single hand-picked file and it imports just that.
  • This is controlled by Handle External File Drops (Preferences → Import → Advanced, on by default). Turn it off to hand OS drops back to Houdini or other tools.

What's covered

External drops work over the network editor while the panel is open: not the viewport, not parameter fields, and not while the panel is closed or hidden behind another tab. Recognized files (textures/HDRIs/models) are claimed; anything else passes straight through to Houdini.

JElib follows your context: drop into a LOP/Solaris network and it builds USD, drop into OBJ and it builds SOP-based geo and a matnet. With Import Into Active Network on (Preferences → Import → Advanced), it imports where you already are.

docs.title: Pick your renderer first
docs.text: The renderer selector in the toolbar (Karma · Redshift · Octane) decides which material JElib builds. Your choice is remembered, so it's always your engine on launch.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
Asset What JElib builds Model / geometry a geo object with a file or Alembic SOP chain, or a dedicated glTF chain for .gltf/.glb PBR texture set / material a material network for your renderer Substance archive (.sbsar) a material network, built from its baked maps (Substance archives) HDRI a dome light Color palette a ramp or gradient node; you pick the form (Color palettes) Saved material / node tree the saved shader, rebuilt for its renderer USD model a reference (or sublayer) into the stage

Importing from the Local Library keeps $HIP/tex/… and $HIP/geo/… paths, so the hip and its assets travel to another machine or artist without relinking.

Models can bring their own materials

An OBJ with its .mtl, an FBX, or a glTF/GLB supplies the materials JElib builds: one shader per material slot, instead of one from the folder's texture set. See Supported file formats.

docs.title: Replace an existing material
docs.text:
Select one or more material containers in the network editor and import a material with Shift held (Shift-drop, or Shift+Load): instead of adding a sibling, JElib rebuilds the selected material in place (same spot in the network, named after the new material) and repoints existing assignments so your objects keep their material. Without Shift, selected material containers are left unchanged and a new material is created. Dropping onto geometry assigns the new material to that geometry, replacing its existing assignment.

Shift-dropping several assets onto several selected materials replaces them pairwise, in the order you read the network (top-to-bottom, left-to-right). Extra assets import as new; extra selected materials are left untouched.

Diving inside a material container works without Shift: importing there always rebuilds that material in place.

docs.title: Import options (preview panel)
docs.text:
Select an asset and use the preview panel's Import Settings to override Preferences without changing their defaults. With several cards selected, a per-asset change follows selected assets of the same kind. Cards without the chosen LOD, resolution or USD Import option keep their own setting.

First select the model card. Its controls then appear in the Import Settings panel at the right of the Browser:

  1. Turn on Create Instances to build a ready-to-edit scatter setup, with VEX distribution and wind controls (model/plant/atlas). See Instance a model, plant, or atlas.
  2. Choose the Instance method: Copy to Points (default), Point Instancer (H22) or Scatter Instances (H22). Both it and the Create Instances toggle stay where you set them as you click through cards.
  3. Click Load into Scene.

The rest of the panel:

  • Material Only — build just the shader, no geometry. Great for reusing a texture set on your own geo.
  • Single USD Node (in Solaris): compatible model and plant selections share one reference or sublayer node, with or without Create Instances. Each asset keeps its settings. Live imports, Loop chains, and conflicting USD namespaces remain separate. The choice stays with you during the session; Preferences sets its default.
  • Loop (rigged/animated FBX and $F sequences only) — repeat the animation for the whole scene range instead of holding on the last frame. See Animation & sequences.
  • Create Material — make a blank material network even when no textures were detected.
  • Import as Atlas — route a packed texture through the Atlas Splitter so decals and leaf cards land on a grid instead of a flat plane.
  • LOD — pick a level of detail when the asset ships several.
  • UV Mode / Resolution — projection and texture resolution for the material.
  • USD Import (in Solaris) — how non-USD geo enters the stage: USD Auto Import, SOP Create, Component Builder, Build USD, or Use Cached USD. Defaults live in Preferences → USD.

Full control-by-control detail is on the Browse tab reference.

docs.title: Instance a model, plant, or atlas
docs.text:
Turn on Create Instances (offered for models, plants, and atlases) and JElib does more than import the asset: it builds a scatter setup that auto-distributes the asset as instances, with VEX controls to shape the spread and even add wind.

Copies are packed primitives, so scattering thousands stays light. The asset is wired in as the prototype on its own input, kept separate from the scatter points.

For a compatible multi-selection of models, JElib builds one shared instancer with the selected models as sources, in both SOPs and Solaris. Select the cards, turn on Create Instances, then load or drop them together.

Start on a demo grid, then repoint it

By default it scatters onto a demo grid, a starting point that isn't scene-aware. Wire your own geometry into the WIRE_USER_POINTS_HERE object merge and flip the switch_points_source switch to distribute across real points instead. In Solaris both nodes sit inside the instancer unless Instance Setup is set to a separate SOP Create node.

Distribution controls live as parameters on the generated wrangle nodes:

  • Variant / Piece — which piece each instance gets (Random or Step). Atlas cards, plant variants, and multi-mesh pieces each become a selectable variant.
  • Pscale — random per-instance scale (size min/max, exponent, seed).
  • Rotation — up-axis, cone angle, random rotation range, snap-to-90°, seeds.

Motion / wind — a wind control adds animated sway, off by default. Dial Directional Amplitude + Wind Direction for a steady lean, or Evolution Amplitude with Frequency and Speed for noise-driven motion.

Time offset — when the asset is itself animated (a $F sequence or an animated Alembic), a time-offset wrangle staggers the copies so they don't all play the same frame at once: Start Frame, Spread Mode (Random / Step / Attribute), Spread, Loop, Seed. Full detail on Animation & sequences.

Atlas & plant specifics

Atlas cards each become a variant. This needs the Atlas Splitter HDA installed; without it, the whole grid is copied and JElib warns you. A plain single-mesh model with no variant attributes scatters as a single prototype. In Solaris, instancing builds a native USD PointInstancer instead.

docs.title: Where materials are built
docs.text: By default JElib builds the material in whatever network you're viewing. Switch to a fixed home in Preferences → Import → Material Network; see Renderers & materials for what each setting does.

docs.title: Import your first asset
docs.text: With a library set up, getting an asset into your scene is a single drag & drop. JElib builds the nodes and creates the material for you. No manual setup needed.

docs.title: 1. Choose your renderer
docs.text:
At the top right of the panel is the renderer selector. Currently Karma, Redshift & Octane are supported. Select the engine you want, and JElib builds your materials for it.

Tip

Your choice is remembered across sessions, so pick once and it's always your engine on launch. Switch it whenever you need to; the change applies for your next import.

docs.title: 2. Drag an asset into your scene
docs.text:
From the Browse grid, drag any asset into Houdini's network editor or directly into the viewport. JElib catches the drop and builds the right nodes in place.

Two other ways to import:

  • Double-click an asset, or select it and press Enter.
  • Select it, then click Load into Scene in the preview panel.

docs.title: 3. Asset types
docs.text:
JElib supports a wide range of asset types that you can import:

Asset What JElib builds Model / geometry a geo object with a file or Alembic SOP chain (a dedicated glTF chain for .gltf/.glb) PBR texture set / material a material network for your renderer Substance archive (.sbsar) a material network, built from its baked maps (Substance archives) HDRI a dome light Color palette a ramp or gradient node (Color palettes) Saved material / node tree the saved shader, rebuilt for its renderer USD model a reference (or sublayer) into the stage

Next: Import into your scene covers every asset type JElib understands and every option along the way, from Material Only to texture atlases.

docs.title: How to install
docs.text: JElib installs in a couple of minutes: run the installer and it does the work, or place the package file yourself.

docs.title: Automatic install
docs.text:
1. Unzip the JElib folder anywhere: the installer copies it to a stable location for you.
  2. Run the installer:
    • Windows — double-click Install_JElib_Windows.bat. If SmartScreen warns, click More info → Run anyway.
    • macOS — double-click Install_JElib_macOS.command. The first time, macOS may say "unidentified developer": right-click → Open → Open.
    • Any OS fallback — run it with Houdini's Python: "<Houdini>/bin/hython" setup_jelib.py
  3. Answer the prompts (mostly just press Enter). The installer detects your Houdini version, copies the code to ~/Documents/JElib, and writes the package config into Houdini's packages folder.
  4. Restart Houdini, then open JElib → Asset Browser.

docs.title: Manual install
docs.text:
1. Copy JElib.json from the unzipped folder into Houdini's packages/ directory, substituting your Houdini version for 21.0:
    • Windows — ~/Documents/houdini21.0/packages/
    • macOS — ~/Library/Preferences/houdini/21.0/packages/
  2. Set the JELIB value in that file to the full path of your unzipped JElib folder. It ships as EDIT_ME_TO_JELIB_ROOT_ABSOLUTE_PATH.
  3. Restart Houdini, then open JElib → Asset Browser.

Either way, JElib asks where your assets are on first launch. See Adding your libraries.

Requires Houdini 20.5, 21.x, or 22.x

JElib runs on the Python these ship (3.11 on 20.5/21.x, 3.13 on 22.x). On older Houdini builds the panel and menu simply won't appear.

docs.title: Color palettes
docs.text: A color palette is a swatch file, the kind you export from Photoshop, Procreate, Coolors, or a brand style guide. JElib reads it, shows it as a swatch grid in the browser. You can then import the colors as regular Color SOPs or as ramps (VEX, Karma, Redshift, Octane).

docs.title: Adding palettes
docs.text:
Drop swatch files into any folder JElib scans and they show up, badged PAL with a swatch-grid thumbnail.

Supported files:

Format Extension Adobe Swatch Exchange .ase GIMP palette .gpl Photoshop swatches .aco Procreate swatches .swatches Plain hex list .txt (only if the name contains palette, colors, swatch, pantone, hex…)

Adding a file to a scanned folder is all it takes, or save one straight from the scene, see Saving a palette below.

RGB swatches only

JElib reads RGB colors from .ase/.aco files; swatches authored in CMYK, LAB, or grayscale are skipped.

docs.title: Importing a palette
docs.text:
A palette isn't a finished material: it's a building block. Drag one in (or Load into Scene) and JElib asks how you want it, via the Load Palette dialog, one of five outputs:

Output What you get Color SOP (one node per color) a color SOP per swatch, good for assigning flat colors to geo VEX Ramp (default) an attribwrangle with a color ramp driving @Cd Redshift / Karma / Octane Ramp a gradient node for that renderer

The dialog lists the three renderer ramps separately. All of them are created inside a matnet named color_palette, ready to plug into a shader as a color source. You can build any of them whatever your active renderer is: the choice decides the node, not the scene.

A supported ramp means an RSRamp, a Karma ramp, an Octane gradient, a Color SOP in Ramp from Attribute mode, or an attribwrangle with a color ramp.

Apply straight to a ramp you already have

Select a single supported ramp node first, then load the palette. JElib skips the dialog and writes the colors straight into that node.

Inside a material builder (a Redshift or Octane vopnet, a USD material builder, or a MaterialX subnet in a Material Library) there's no dialog either: JElib creates that renderer's ramp right there in the builder.

docs.title: How the colors map
docs.text:
Each swatch becomes one ramp key, in file order, evenly spaced across the ramp with linear interpolation, so you get a smooth gradient between colors, not hard bands. There's no limit on the number of colors.

A selected palette's preview panel adds a ramp-interpolation picker: Linear ramp by default, or Constant ramp for hard bands between colors, plus the rest of Houdini's basis set.

Colors are converted to ACEScg for the Color SOP, VEX, Redshift, and Karma outputs; the Octane output uses linear sRGB.

The preview panel shows a Colors: N count for a selected palette. The material and geometry import toggles (Material Only, LOD, and so on) don't apply to palettes.

docs.title: Saving a palette
docs.text:
Palettes go the other way too. Select ramp nodes or Color SOPs and save them like any other node setup: right-click → Save Asset [JE], or drag them onto a folder in the nav tree or onto the grid (see Save to the browser). When every selected node is a Color SOP or a supported ramp, JElib writes an .ase swatch file instead of a node asset. It appears as a palette card right away, loads into any of the five outputs, and opens in Photoshop or Illustrator.

  • A ramp becomes one swatch per key, in ramp order, named <node>_01, <node>_02, … Key positions aren't kept: a palette is an ordered list, and loading it back spaces the colors evenly.
  • A Color SOP set to Constant becomes one swatch, named after the node; set to Ramp from Attribute its ramp is saved like any other ramp. The other Color Types have no color of their own, so a selection containing one is saved as a node asset instead.
  • A key hidden under another key at the very start or end of a ramp (an RSRamp's default black and white, say, with your own keys dragged on top) isn't part of the gradient you see, so it isn't saved either.
  • Colors are converted back from ACEScg to sRGB (Octane gradients from linear sRGB), the reverse of loading. A swatch file is 8-bit sRGB, so a color outside the sRGB gamut is clipped on the way out.

Mix in anything else (a box, a subnet, a shader) and the selection is saved as a regular node asset instead. Nothing asks; the nodes decide.

docs.title: Parameter menus
docs.text: JElib adds two items to the right-click menu of any string parameter in Houdini, handy for jumping to files and keeping paths portable. Right-click any file/path parameter to access them directly at the top of the menu:

docs.title: Open Folder [JE]
docs.text: Reveals the parameter's file in Explorer/Finder. It expands the value first, so $VAR, $F, and <UDIM> tokens resolve to the real location. You land in the actual folder without decoding the expression by hand. If the expanded path is a file it's selected; otherwise its containing folder opens.

docs.title: Convert to Relative/Absolute Path [JE]
docs.text:
One click flips the path between a portable $VAR-relative form (e.g. $ASSETS/wood/oak.exr) and a concrete absolute path, whichever applies. It recognises the studio roots $JOB, $ASSETS, $HIP, $STUDIO, and the vendor library roots, and picks the most specific match. Frame and UDIM tokens are left intact.

Select several string parameters and it converts them all at once.

Why it matters

Relative paths survive moving the project or handing the file to another machine or artist; absolute paths are handy for debugging or pasting elsewhere. This is the same portability idea as Use Relative Path on libraries, applied to any parameter.

docs.title: Promote to OBJ
docs.text: Pull any SOP node out to its own object at OBJ level, without moving or copying the original network. Handy for building render, layout or simulation objects from pieces buried inside a bigger geometry object.

docs.title: How to promote
docs.text:
Right-click a SOP node and choose Promote to OBJ [JE]. JElib asks for a name prefix, then places the new object next to the geometry object that holds the node, inside the same OBJ subnet if there is one.

It creates a geometry object with an Object Merge that points back at the node, so the new object updates whenever the source changes. The original node, its network and its display flags stay exactly as they were.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: New objects are named with a prefix plus the node name: promoting crate gives RENDER_crate. Change the prefix in the dialog, or leave it empty to use the node name alone. The dialog remembers your last prefix for the rest of the session. If the name is taken, Houdini adds its usual number.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
The new object starts exactly where the source sits in the world, including any transforms on parent objects and subnets. After that it is independent: move it freely.

A snapshot of the source's position

The new object copies the source object's transform once. If you later move or animate the source object at OBJ level, the promoted object doesn't follow. Changes to the geometry itself always come through.

docs.title: Browse tab
docs.text:
The Browse tab is the main workspace: a toolbar, the asset grid, a preview panel, and the navigation tree. It has two ways to navigate a library:

  • Grid view shows the assets in the current folder, ready to browse, search, select, and load.
  • Browse view shows the current folder's subfolders first. Open a folder tile to drill down; use Backspace to go back up.
Grid viewBrowse and select assets. Browse viewDrill into library folders.

For the how do I browse/search/filter/favorite workflow, see Find & organize; this page covers everything else on the tab.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Left to right:

Control What it does Collection field Search and jump to a saved collection. Type to autocomplete; the dropdown arrow lists all collections. Search · Filter · Favorites Covered in Find & organize. Browse Toggle Finder-style drill-down. See Find & organize. Maps Show individual texture maps instead of grouped sets. View Switch between grid and list view. Thumbnail size Slider, 64–512 px. Double-click to reset. Renderer Active renderer for material and texture imports. Your pick is remembered across sessions; this selector is the setting. Reload Reload libraries. Shift-click to force-rescan all. A plain click fully re-checks every NAS library; local ones are re-checked only when their folder changed. See Remote & synced libraries for the per-library opt-outs.

When any filter is active, a chip row appears below the toolbar with a Clear all link.

docs.title: The asset grid
docs.text:
Each card shows a thumbnail, the asset name (elided if long), and a type badge (EXR, FBX, VDB, RS, UDIM, SEQ, ANIM / RIG for a rigged FBX, a category, or a renderer name for saved materials). Overlays: a renderer logo (bottom-left, plus a usd logo for USD-backed assets), the favorite star, and a small dot showing cloud/sync state (hover the dot for a plain explanation).

Interaction

  • Click an asset to load it into the preview panel.
  • Double-click an asset to load it into the scene; double-click a folder tile to enter it.
  • Ctrl / Shift-click to multi-select.
  • Keyboard — arrow keys, Home/End and Page Up/Down move the selection (the preview follows); Enter loads the selected asset(s) or enters a folder tile; Backspace goes up one folder in Browse mode.
  • Drag assets out of the grid to drop them into your scene.

docs.title: Right-click an asset
docs.text:
Item Action New Directory… / New Sub-Directory… Make a folder (with …and Move N Assets… variants in your own libraries). Open Source Folder Reveal the asset in Explorer/Finder. Copy Path / Copy Relative Path Copy the file path. Delete Asset… Delete the asset (writable libraries only). Make Available Offline / Make Online-only Cache or un-cache the asset locally (on-demand libraries). Generate Thumbnail Render a thumbnail for the asset. Set Thumbnail… Choose your own image for the asset. Open Thumbnail Folder / Delete Thumbnail Manage its cached thumbnail. Delete USD Cache Remove the baked .usd sidecar.

Right-clicking a folder tile instead offers Open Folder, New / Rename / Delete Directory… (in writable libraries).

docs.title: Preview panel
docs.text:
Selecting an asset fills the preview panel on the right:

  • Thumbnail and name at the top.
  • Asset Info — type · format · size, local-cache status, per-type details (colors, nodes, channels, UDIM tiles, frames…), and clickable tag pills (click a tag to search it).
  • USD — cache state and prim/variant/material info, when relevant.

  • Import Settings — per-asset options shown only when they apply: LOD, USD Import mode, Resolution, UV Mode, the instance method (Copy to Points / Point Instancer / Scatter Instances (H22)), Loop (any asset baking to animated USD: rigged/animated FBX or an $F sequence), and toggles for Create Instances, Material Only, Create Material, and Import as Atlas.

    Create Instances and the instance method are sticky: the choice carries to the next card you click. Create Instances is unavailable (and says why) on an .abc frame sequence; see Animation & sequences.

The primary Load into Scene button (bottom) imports the asset with those settings. With Material Only ticked it loads just the shader, no geometry.

Per-asset overrides

Import Settings override Preferences defaults. With several cards selected, changing a per-asset control applies it to selected assets of the same kind. A card without the chosen LOD, resolution or USD Import option keeps its own valid setting. Create Instances and the instance method remain sticky across cards; the model picker stays specific to its kit.

docs.title: Navigation tree
docs.text:
The left tree mirrors your libraries and their folders. Names show uppercased, with optional asset counts (toggle in Preferences). Favorites appears at the top whenever you have favorites, and Local Library pins near the top when Show Local Library ($HIP) is on and a tex or geo folder sits next to the current scene file.

Right-click a folder for:

Item Action Open Folder · Copy Path Reveal or copy the folder. New / Rename / Delete Directory… Manage folders (writable libraries). Reload This Library Rescan just this library; always checks the source fully, even when Trust Cache on Reload is on. Sequence Detection Choose Use Browser Default, Group as Sequences or Keep Files Separate for this folder. See Browser Display. Trust Cache on Reload (NAS libraries only) Skip re-checking this library on a plain Reload. See Remote & synced libraries. Make Available Offline Cache the whole folder (on-demand libraries). Disable on This Machine Turn the library off locally. Scan on This Machine (any folder or collection below the root) Uncheck to stop scanning it here. It stays in the tree as a dimmed (not scanned) entry; right-click it again to re-include it. Works on vendor collections too (a single Greyscalegorilla material pack), where JElib skips that pack's folders by their shared name prefix. Per machine, so a NAS-bound laptop can skip an unused vendor subfolder (a Greyscalegorilla hdris, say) while a workstation keeps it. Not offered where a collection's folders can't be told apart from its neighbours' (some Quixel categories). Hide the dimmed entries with Show Unscanned Folders in Preferences. Remove from Browser Drop the library from the list (files untouched).

docs.title: Libraries tab
docs.text:
The Libraries tab is where you add, remove, and manage the folders JElib scans for assets. Each row is one library.

For the concepts behind base folders and portable paths, see Adding your libraries. This page is the control-by-control reference.

docs.title: The library table
docs.text:
Libraries are listed in a three-column table:

Column Shows Name the library's display name (double-click to rename) Path its folder (double-click to edit; hover for the full path) Status scan result; see below

Drag a row to reorder it, or use the ↑ / ↓ buttons in the footer (Move library up / Move library down). Order here is the order libraries appear in the nav tree.

Ctrl- or Shift-click selects multiple rows; the right-click actions (Disable / Enable on This Machine, Remove) then apply to the whole selection at once.

docs.title: What Status means
docs.text:
Status Meaning 1,234 assets found (the count) 0 folder exists but is empty … still scanning Cloud a cloud folder that's paused or still syncing Not found the folder is missing No path no path set yet Disabled turned off on this machine

Hover the count on a NAS library with Trust Cache on Reload turned on (Remote & synced libraries) for a reminder that a plain Reload won't check that library for changes.

docs.title: Add a library
docs.text: Add… in the footer opens the folder picker (Select Library Folder). The new library is named after the folder and starts editable and writable. See Adding your libraries for the three ways to add one.

docs.title: Remove a library
docs.text: Select a row and click Remove, or right-click the row → Remove Library (with several rows selected: Remove N Libraries, one undo step). There's no confirmation, but it's undoable (Ctrl+Z). Removing a library only drops it from the list; it never touches the files on disk.

docs.title: The Selected Library inspector
docs.text:
Select a row to open the Selected Library pane on the right (drag the divider to collapse it). It exposes everything about that one library:

Path

  • The folder path, with a chooser button (Select Library Folder).
  • Use Relative Path rewrites the path with a matching Houdini variable so your config stays portable across machines. When several variables match, choose the one you want from the menu. It toggles to Use Absolute Path. See Adding your libraries.
  • The / button flips between forward slashes and backslashes.

Toggles

  • Read-Only Library — treat the library as managed by an external tool. Disables folder drag-move, new folder, delete, and drops. Auto-set for Greyscalegorilla / Quixel / Fab on first run.
  • Enabled on This Machine — turn the library on or off for this computer only. Saved locally; your synced library list is unchanged.
  • Expand in Nav Tree — start this library expanded (uncheck to start collapsed).
  • Enable On-Demand Caching — copy assets locally on demand from a remote root. When on, set the Remote Source Root below.

Remote Source Root (when caching is on) — the remote/cloud path assets are pulled from.

Local files (when caching is on) — Measure reports everything under the library's local path on disk: the local cache plus any always-local files (size and file count). Make Online-only… frees that space by deleting only files verified to still exist on the remote; anything not mirrored survives, the remote is never touched, and files re-download on next use. See Remote & cloud libraries.

Ignore Pattern / Ignore Directories — chips that exclude matching files or folders from scanning.

Notes — free text; saves itself a moment after you stop typing.

Read-only vendor libraries

Greyscalegorilla, Quixel, and Fab libraries are flagged Read-Only automatically; JElib never writes into those trees. On-demand caching still works for them, because it only reads the remote and writes to your local cache.

docs.title: Re-run setup
docs.text: Re-run setup… (footer) reopens the first-run welcome flow to re-detect your assets folder and add any libraries it finds. It's additive: it never removes or rewrites libraries you already have.

docs.title: Download Missing Assets
docs.text: Download Missing Assets (footer) reads the current scene, finds assets that come from an on-demand library and aren't cached on this machine yet, and pulls them from the remote source, for opening a scene whose assets were never cached here. Needs On-Demand Caching on This Machine and a library with a Remote Source Root. See Remote & cloud libraries.

docs.title: Show Local Library ($HIP)
docs.text:
The Show Local Library ($HIP) checkbox (footer) surfaces a Local Library at the top of the nav tree whenever a tex or geo folder sits next to the current scene file. It follows the scene when you open or save a scene, and is not listed when neither folder exists. It never appears in the library table.

Its tex and geo folders are separate browse roots. You can organize assets in subfolders below either root. Imports keep portable $HIP/tex/… or $HIP/geo/… paths, so the scene and its assets travel together. New files appear on Reload because this library is always scanned fresh.

docs.title: Startup collection
docs.text:
The Startup dropdown (footer, right) picks a collection to auto-select the next time the panel opens. It's filled from your nav tree after each scan.

No manual rescan needed

There's no Scan button here: editing a path, adding or removing a library, or toggling Enabled rescans automatically. The Status column always reflects the latest scan.

docs.title: Preferences tab
docs.text:
Every setting on the Preferences tab applies live: there's no Save or Apply button, and nothing needs a restart. Settings are grouped top to bottom as below.

Reset a single setting

Ctrl+Middle-click any control to reset just that one to its default. The Reset to Defaults button (bottom right) resets them all; library paths are never touched.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: Setting What it does Theme Visual theme. Default inherits Houdini's look; on Houdini 22 it follows your live color theme (Edit ▸ Color Theme), accent and all, updating as you edit it. Minimal, Neutral (hueless greys, with thumbnails the only colour), and XSI (Softimage-inspired) are bundled skins. Add your own as a bundle folder in the plugin's themes/, as <name>/theme.json. Keep Window Above Other Apps When the browser floats in its own window, keep it above every other application's windows, not just Houdini's. No effect while docked in a pane. Saved per machine; the default matches your platform's native behavior (on for macOS, off for Windows).

docs.title: Browser Display
docs.text:
Expand Browser Display under Appearance for these settings:

Setting What it does Default Show Asset Counts Append counts to nav-tree labels, e.g. Metals (42). Off Show Asset Count Footer Show the total asset count in a footer under the Browse view. On Show Unscanned Folders Keep folders excluded with Scan on This Machine visible as dimmed (not scanned) entries. On Sequence Detection Group numbered files into sequence cards or keep them separate. Auto-detect recognizes animation formats; a folder can override the browser setting from its right-click menu. Auto-detect

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
How assets come into your scene.

Setting Options Default Material Network Current Network (build where you're viewing: a per-asset matnet at the cursor, or directly inside a matnet/vopnet; /mat in a non-material context) · Global (shared /mat) · OBJ Context (a shared /obj/matnet) · SOP Context (per-asset matnet inside the geo network) Current Network Material Assignment shop_materialpath (explicit per-prim path) · Name Attribute (group by name string) shop_materialpath Material Type Standard Material · Open PBR Material Standard Material Bump Map Mode Normal Map · Bump Map · Displacement Normal Map (bump falls back when no normal exists) Default Projection UV · Triplanar (per-material override lives in the preview panel) UV Default LOD LOD 0 (highest detail) · Lowest Detail · High / Source Mesh LOD 0

The renderer has no preference: the toolbar selector is remembered across sessions, so your last choice is your engine on every launch.

Default LOD is where a multi-LOD asset starts: the inspector's LOD picker and folder drops from Explorer/Finder both default here. High / Source Mesh applies when the asset ships an unreduced source (e.g. Quixel High) and falls back to LOD 0 otherwise.

docs.title: Advanced
docs.text:
Collapsed by default; click Advanced to expand.

Setting What it does Default Import Into Active Network Import inside the network you're already in, if it's compatible; otherwise create a new container at the top level. On Default Create Instances Default state for the per-asset Create Instances toggle; it auto-adds a scatter chain to atlas/model/plant drops. Off Relative Material Node Path Store shop_materialpath as a relative node path (../matnet/shader) instead of absolute. On Force Absolute File Paths Write absolute OS paths into the scene instead of $VAR/… tokens. Off Handle External File Drops Import textures, PBR sets, HDRIs, and models dragged from your OS file manager onto the network editor (while this panel is open). Off hands those drops back to Houdini. On Prefer 16-bit Textures When a set ships 8- and 16-bit versions of a map, pick 16-bit. Applies on the next library refresh. Off Name Texture Nodes After File Name texture nodes after the texture file (extension stripped) instead of the channel (basecolor, normal, …). Applies to newly imported materials. Off Viewport Drop Targets Hit Component A material dropped on geometry in the Scene Viewer goes to the part under the cursor (material slot / named part in OBJ, GeomSubset in Solaris), or the whole object when no part is found. Ctrl+drop flips this for one drop. On Ask Multi-Piece Scatter Ask whether a model made of several separate objects scatters them individually or stays in one piece. Off, JElib decides from the object names. Off

docs.title: USD
docs.text:
How non-USD geometry (see Supported file formats) enters a Solaris/LOPs stage.

Setting Options Default USD Import Mode Auto · SOP Create · Component Builder · Bake .usd Auto USD Import As Reference · Sublayer Reference Prefer Mtlx Builder Build materials generated by Stage drops in a USD MaterialX Builder, whatever renderer is selected. With this off, Karma uses a Karma Material Builder. Applies to model, plant, atlas and material imports, including Houdini's native Stage galleries. The override follows Material Type: Standard Surface or OpenPBR. Houdini 20.5 lacks OpenPBR, so it uses Standard Surface for either choice, which may render as a simpler preview in Redshift and Octane. VDB volumes keep the selected renderer's volume shader; saved USD files and node trees keep their authored materials. Off Single USD Node Compatible model and plant selections share one reference or sublayer node, with or without Create Instances. Live imports, Loop chains, and conflicting USD namespaces keep separate nodes. The preview has a session choice; Preferences supplies its default. On Instance Method Copy to Points · Point Instancer (H22) · Scatter Instances (H22): the Stage instance method a new Create Instances toggle starts from, and which LOP a Solaris import builds. It is sticky: changing it in the preview panel carries to the cards you select next. Copy to Points Instance Setup Inside the instancer · Separate SOP Create node: where a Solaris Create Instances chain builds the SOP network that scatters its instance points. A separate SOP Create node lets you see and repoint the points in the LOP network. Inside the instancer Use Baked Cache Reference an up-to-date baked .usd directly instead of rebuilding the Component Builder chain. On Proxy Detail (%) Polyreduce percentage for the proxy purpose when baking (1–100). Also caps the collision (simproxy) hulls. Animated $F sequences bake neither. 20 Cache to $HIP Write USD caches under $HIP/usd/… instead of next to the source asset, handy when the library folder is read-only or you'll collect with the hip later. Off Add Renderer Suffix Include the renderer in geometry USD names, such as Asset_Karma.usd. Turn it off to use Asset.usd; baking with another renderer replaces that shared file. Applies to live Component Builder output too. On Clean Up After Bake After baking, remove the Component Builder nodes and leave just the reference/sublayer. On

Import Mode in brief

Auto bakes a sidecar .usd when the source folder is writable, else falls back to SOP Create (no disk write). Component Builder builds a live chain. Bake .usd always writes <asset_dir>/usd/<name>.usd. A rigged/animated FBX has its own skeleton-aware modes. See Animation & sequences.

docs.title: Geometry Import
docs.text:
Simple Import (off by default) brings geometry in as just a file/Alembic SOP plus an OUT null, skipping the xform, attribdelete, material, matchsize, and connectivity nodes.

Split Pieces — what happens when a model is made of several named objects:

Option What you get Off One output for the whole model. SOP Network (default) One extra output per named piece inside the geo. OBJ Network A subnet holding the import plus one geometry object per piece.

Greyed out while Simple Import is on; that mode builds no chain to split.

Below it, one card per format (FBX, OBJ, ABC), each with the same four controls:

Control Options FBX OBJ ABC Scale import scale (e.g. 0.01 = cm→m) 0.01 0.01 0.01 Match Size None · Match Size · Match Size (Auto Scale) None None None Attrib Delete strip helper/detail attributes On Off Off Material SOP build the Material SOP On On On

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Setting What it does On-Demand Caching on This Machine Per-machine master switch: pull remote-backed libraries into a local cache as you use them. Leave off on a machine that already has the assets locally. See Remote & cloud libraries. Trust Cloud Library Cache Without Verifying Skip re-checking cloud-synced libraries (Dropbox / Google Drive / OneDrive / iCloud Drive / Synology Drive) for changes on every reload: much faster on a slow mount, but a plain Reload won't notice new or removed files. Off by default; saved per machine. See Remote & cloud libraries. Prefetch Selected Cloud / NAS Assets While browsing, download the selected asset from its remote source in the background so dropping it is instant. On-demand libraries only; saved per machine. Thumbnail Cache Folder for the pre-scaled thumbnail cache. Defaults to $JE_ASSET_BROWSER_CACHE (set in the package JSON). Auto-generate on Save Render a geometry thumbnail automatically when a 3D asset is saved via Save Asset…. Right-click → Generate Thumbnail always works regardless.

Two buttons: Cache Thumbnails pre-scales every preview into the cache; Clear Cache deletes pre-scaled thumbnails and generated geometry, material, HDRI, and texture previews. For the full workflow (and the difference between generating and caching), see Make thumbnails.

docs.title: Thumbnail Appearance
docs.text:
Controls how generated thumbnails look. See Make thumbnails.

Setting Options / effect Default Caption Alignment Center · Left · Right Center Use Simple Sphere Render on a plain sphere instead of the shaderball, better for tiling materials. Off Use HDRI Light the preview with an HDRI instead of the default studio lights. Off HDRI Path Custom HDRI file (enabled when Use HDRI is on). Leave empty for the HDA default. HDA default

docs.title: Asset Variable
docs.text: The picker at the bottom of the tab sets the $JELIB_ASSETS root: the variable libraries resolve through. See Adding your libraries.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
Collapsed by default, at the bottom of the tab.

Setting What it does Default Debug Logging Print diagnostic detail to the Python Shell: why a library re-scanned, which thumbnails failed to load, errors that are otherwise silent. JELIB_DEBUG=1 in the environment does the same for a session that cannot reach this panel. Off Copy Diagnostics (button) Copy build, Houdini, library and environment details plus the most recent log lines to the clipboard, ready to paste into a bug report. Works with Debug Logging off, but only what was logged since the panel opened is included. —

docs.title: Remote & cloud libraries
docs.text: Your libraries don't have to live on the local disk. JElib works with libraries on cloud storage (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Synology Drive) and on a NAS / remote source, including files that are online-only (no local copy yet). It scans them safely and pulls files down only when you actually use them.

docs.title: Two flavours
docs.text:
• Cloud-sync folders (Dropbox / Google Drive / OneDrive / iCloud Drive / Synology Drive) — files may be online-only placeholders. JElib browses them and pulls on load. Cloud is pull-only: it can fetch a placeholder but can't evict it back.
  • NAS / remote source with on-demand caching — a master copy lives on the remote; a local cache mirrors it as you use assets. This one you can pull and push back to online-only.

docs.title: Safe scanning
docs.text: JElib scans cloud and NAS libraries from their file listing only. It reads small metadata and existing preview images, never the heavy textures/geo/HDRIs. So adding a big cloud library won't mass-download it. Heavy files stay online-only until you load them.

docs.title: Availability at a glance
docs.text:
Every asset shows where it lives:

Where you see it Meaning Asset card ✓ Synced locally, ready Asset card ☁ Remote-only but reachable, downloads on load Asset card ! Remote unreachable, can't load until reconnected Preview panel Cache state, Synced or Online-only Libraries tab, Status Cloud = folder present but empty (still syncing/paused)

Hover the ☁ dot for a plain-language reason (e.g. Online-only — files download on first load).

docs.title: Importing an online-only asset
docs.text:
JElib downloads the asset first, then builds the nodes:

  • Cloud placeholders download before the import, with a cancelable Downloading… X / Y MB dialog. If the source is offline it stops cleanly and loads nothing, rather than half-importing.
  • NAS / on-demand libraries download in the background. Keep browsing while the files pull; the import fires the moment they land. Load more assets and they queue behind it. The preview panel's cache line tracks progress (Caching … X / Y MB · 1 queued · Esc cancels); Esc cancels the download and every queued import, and switching to a different scene cancels them too. An import never lands in a scene you didn't load it into. Files that finished downloading stay cached either way.

    Prefetch while you browse

    Turn on Prefetch Selected Cloud / NAS Assets (Preferences → Caching) and JElib starts pulling the selected asset in the background as you browse, so dropping it is instant. The preview panel's cache line counts it down live (Prefetching… X / Y MB → Synced).

docs.title: Setting up an on-demand (NAS) library
docs.text: The master files stay on the NAS. A folder on your own disk holds the copies JElib pulls down as you import them. Imports point at that local folder, so they keep working while the NAS is offline.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the two folders
docs.text:
Connect to your NAS and open its asset folder in Explorer or Finder (on macOS, mount the share before you start JElib). Then choose a writable folder on your own disk for the cache; it can start empty.

These are the two folders, using a NAS share and a local disk as examples:

Folder Windows macOS Remote source folder //NAS/assets /Volumes/assets Local cache folder D:/AssetCache /Users/you/Documents/JElib_Assets

Each library gets its own folder inside both, named after the library, so Lookdev Archive becomes //NAS/assets/Lookdev Archive on the NAS and D:/AssetCache/Lookdev Archive locally.

Both folders mirror the same structure, so Models/Gallery Bench.bgeo.sc on the NAS lands at the same relative path inside the local library. Keep the two folders separate; never put one inside the other.

The screenshots use synthetic showroom assets with separate NAS/Assets and Local Cache folders. Substitute your own mounted NAS and local cache paths.

docs.title: 2. Set up a new library
docs.text:
On first launch, use Set Up - Asset Libraries. If you already use JElib, open Libraries → Re-run setup… to add another library through this flow.

  1. Click Choose a folder… and pick the remote source folder, such as //NAS/assets or /Volumes/assets.
  2. Tick the library folders to add, such as Lookdev Archive. Double-click a folder if you need to look further inside before choosing.
  3. Tick Cache files locally (Optional).
  4. Set Local cache folder to the local folder you prepared, such as D:/AssetCache. Stop at that folder; JElib adds the library's subfolder itself.
  5. Click Add Libraries. JElib enables caching for this machine and the new libraries, then scans the NAS listing.
First-run setup with Lookdev Archive selected, Cache files locally enabled and a separate local cache folder12345

With the default Asset Variable, setup points $JELIB_ASSETS at the local cache folder and $JELIB_ASSETS_REMOTE at the remote source folder. Each library's remote path is derived from those, so you never enter it by hand.

docs.title: 3. Check both caching switches
docs.text:
A library added through the setup above already has both switches on. For an existing library, follow these steps:

  1. Open Preferences and scroll to Caching.

  2. Turn on On-Demand Caching on This Machine. This choice is saved on this computer and takes effect immediately.

    Preferences scrolled to Caching with On-Demand Caching on This Machine enabled and prefetch disabled2

  3. Open Libraries and select the library. To add an empty cache folder as a new library instead, click Add… and choose that folder.

  4. In Selected Library, set Path to this library's local cache folder, such as D:/AssetCache/Lookdev Archive. Use the folder chooser beside Path or edit the field and press Enter.
  5. Turn on Enable On-Demand Caching.
  6. Set Remote Source Root to the matching NAS library folder, such as //NAS/assets/Lookdev Archive. Use its folder chooser or edit the field and press Enter. If setup already derives this path, leave it as shown.
Lookdev Archive in the Libraries inspector with a local Path, Enable On-Demand Caching enabled and its NAS Remote Source Root3456

Changing Path updates where JElib looks for local files; it does not move files. Keep any existing master files on the NAS.

docs.title: 4. Test one import
docs.text:
1. In Browse, right-click the library and choose Reload This Library, then select an asset wearing the ☁ badge. That badge means its files are not local yet.

    Gallery Bench before import with an online-only badge and Local cache: Online-only, Prefetch offGallery Bench before import with an online-only badge and Local cache: Online-only, Prefetch off

  2. Double-click to import it. JElib downloads the files first, so give that a moment. The badge becomes a check mark and the preview reads Local cache: Synced.

    Gallery Bench after import with a local availability check mark and Local cache: SyncedGallery Bench after import with a local availability check mark and Local cache: Synced

  3. The imported node's file parameter should now resolve inside your local cache. Expect a path starting with $JELIB_ASSETS; hover the parameter to see where it expands to.

Imported Gallery Bench File SOP showing its Geometry File path inside the local cache Houdini's file browser opened at the local Models folder after import, containing Gallery Bench.bgeo.sc

If Prefetch Selected Cloud / NAS Assets is on in Preferences → Caching, selecting an asset starts downloading it straight away, so you may not see the import do it. Turn prefetch off for this check if you want to watch.

If nothing appears

Check the mounted NAS path and both caching switches, then try Reload This Library again. If an asset stays online-only after an import, check the import status line and confirm that the local cache is writable.

docs.title: Make available offline / online-only
docs.text:
Right-click assets in the grid:

  • Make Available Offline — download the selected assets into the local cache, so importing them later is instant. A library in the nav tree has this too, to download the whole library at once.
  • Make Online-only — (NAS libraries only) delete the local copies to reclaim space. JElib checks that a remote file exists and its size and modification time match the local copy. Files that differ, use linked paths or change before deletion are kept.

To manage a whole library at once, use Measure / Make Online-only… in the Libraries tab inspector, same safety rules, applied library-wide.

docs.title: One config, many machines
docs.text:
Library paths are stored relative to an Asset Variable, so one synced config resolves correctly on every machine. The default is the managed $JELIB_ASSETS; first-run setup and the bottom of Preferences let you pick an existing Houdini variable or name another managed one. Each machine maps it to its own folder.

  • New libraries under the variable's Resolved Folder adopt it automatically. Libraries elsewhere keep absolute paths. Use Relative Path in the Libraries inspector converts one where a matching Houdini variable exists; if several match, pick from the menu.
  • Renaming a JElib-managed variable updates matching library and remote paths without moving folders, and saved scenes keep working under the old name.
  • The first-run setup offers detected cloud providers as one-click picks. For a NAS mirror, point $JELIB_ASSETS_REMOTE at the remote and JElib derives each library's remote from its local path.

Machines without the remote variable read locally

If a library's Remote Source Root starts with a variable that isn't set on the current machine (say $STUDIO_NAS on a laptop that has everything local), JElib simply reads the library from its local folder, live, with no warnings. The only trace is a note on the count in the Libraries tab. Scans on such a machine aren't cached, so set the variable (or clear the Remote Source Root) if it's meant to be permanent.

docs.title: Bringing up a second machine
docs.text:
1. Install JElib as usual (see How to install), then on first run pick where this machine's assets live. Expand Asset Variable to use something other than $JELIB_ASSETS.
  2. Copy or sync user_libraries.json and favorites.json from the first machine. Those two files carry your library list and favorites, not the scan cache. A shared scan cache can skip the first full scan, but the config alone won't.
  3. If this machine caches from a NAS, choose the remote source folder and Cache files locally during setup, then check each library's Path and Remote Source Root. A machine with everything local can leave caching off.
  4. Open the browser and verify one import.

Enable per machine

Enabled on This Machine (Libraries inspector, or Disable on This Machine in the nav tree) turns a library on or off for this computer only. Your synced library list and favorites are untouched.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
Reload re-checks the source by default. A plain Reload click always reads the remote, so it reflects exactly what's there and new or removed files always show up. That accuracy is the slow option on a big or distant NAS. Two per-library settings trade it for speed; both are off by default, so a stale cache is never served unless you asked for it.

  • Trust Cache on Reload — right-click a NAS library in the nav tree. A plain Reload then skips the check and shows the last saved scan, so it won't notice anything added, changed or removed until you force a real one: Shift- or Ctrl-click Reload for every library, or right-click → Reload This Library for just that one. Both gestures ignore the setting.
  • Trust Cloud Library Cache Without Verifying — Preferences → Caching. The same trade for cloud-sync libraries (Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud Drive, Synology Drive).
  • If you never touch part of a vendor library on this machine (a Greyscalegorilla hdris folder on a laptop, say), right-click that folder in the nav tree and uncheck Scan on This Machine. That subtree is never walked, cached, or thumbnailed here again, and your other machines keep scanning it. See the Browse tab reference for the full rules.
  • Only the asset's primary files are pulled. A USD asset that references other files internally, or a saved node-tree material with external textures, pulls its main file. The rest resolve from the remote or may be missing locally. After a load, the cache status line reports anything that stayed remote.
  • Online-only $F image sequences can't be pulled yet — they keep the cloud indicator.
  • Pulled files accumulate — there's no automatic local eviction (use Make Online-only on NAS libraries to reclaim space).

docs.title: Renderers & materials
docs.text: When you import a PBR asset, JElib builds a complete, wired material for your active renderer: every map connected to the right input, in the right color space, ready to render. No manual shader work.

docs.title: Supported renderers
docs.text:
JElib currently supports Karma, Redshift, and Octane, in both the OBJ//mat and LOP/Solaris contexts. Pick your engine with the toolbar renderer selector; your choice is remembered across sessions.

In Solaris, JElib builds inside a materiallibrary; in OBJ, a native material container. Karma imports use a Karma Material Builder by default, so you can add Karma nodes alongside MaterialX nodes. Turn on Prefer Mtlx Builder to create a pure USD MaterialX Builder for materials generated by Stage drops, even when Redshift or Octane is selected. OBJ and /mat imports keep the selected renderer. Existing materials inside USD files and saved node trees are imported as authored.

A model can also bring its own materials, giving one shader per slot instead of one from the folder's texture set (Supported file formats).

If a renderer isn't installed
