If the chosen renderer's plugin isn't loaded, JElib skips the material and still loads the geometry, with no broken nodes. Switch the selector to a renderer you have installed and re-import to get the shader.

docs.title: The material it builds
docs.text:
By default JElib builds each renderer's standard surface. Switch Preferences → Import → Material Type to Open PBR for the OpenPBR surface instead:

Renderer Standard Open PBR Redshift Standard Material OpenPBR Material Octane Standard Surface Open PBR Surface Karma Standard Surface Open PBR Surface

The MaterialX override follows Material Type, choosing Standard Surface or OpenPBR. Houdini 20.5 lacks OpenPBR, so its MaterialX builder uses Standard Surface for either choice; Redshift and Octane may then render the simpler viewport preview instead of the full material.

docs.title: What gets wired
docs.text:
For a full PBR set, JElib connects the maps it finds:

  • Base color, roughness, metalness, specular, opacity, emission
  • Normal / bump / height (see below)
  • Sheen, coat, anisotropy, translucency / SSS when present; a translucency map even switches on subsurface automatically

Color space is handled for you: color maps as sRGB, data maps (roughness, metal, normal, height) as raw. Packed maps (one texture holding several channels) are split to the right inputs, so roughness, metalness and translucency each take their own channel, and a glossiness map is inverted into roughness when no roughness map exists.

AO maps aren't connected

Ambient-occlusion maps are not wired; the standard surfaces have no AO input. Composite AO into your base color beforehand if you need it.

docs.title: Normal, bump & displacement
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Bump Map Mode decides how surface detail is wired:

  • Normal Map (default) — use the normal map; fall back to a bump/height map only when there's no normal map.
  • Bump Map — prefer a dedicated bump map over the normal map.
  • Displacement — route the height map through the renderer's displacement output instead of bump.

Each renderer uses its native nodes for this (Redshift BumpMap/Displacement, Karma mtlxnormalmap/mtlxdisplacement, Octane's normal/bump/displacement slots), and respects a normal-strength value if the set ships one.

docs.title: UV or triplanar
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Default Projection:

  • UV — standard UV sampling, with shared Scale / Offset / Rotate controls on the material.
  • Triplanar — world-space projection, no UV unwrap needed. A triplanar node is inserted per texture; the Scale/Offset/Rotate controls don't apply.

You can also override projection per import in the preview panel.

docs.title: Where the material lives & how it's assigned
docs.text:
Preferences → Import → Material Network controls where the material is built:

Setting Builds into Current Network (default) A per-asset matnet in whatever network you're viewing, or directly inside a matnet/vopnet you're in, falling back to /mat in a non-material context SOP Context The geo network Global A shared /mat OBJ Context A shared /obj/matnet

When replacing an existing geometry assignment, JElib reuses its material network when safe, ahead of this preference.

In OBJ/SOP, a Material SOP assigns the material by shop_materialpath (or by name attribute, see Material Assignment). In Solaris, a materiallibrary → assignmaterial chain does it. Either way JElib also adds viewport-preview textures so the asset shows shaded before you render.

To replace a Solaris material, select its builder in the material network and Shift-drag a new material from the browser. Existing Assign Material LOPs follow the replacement. Scene View drops assign to the picked object; Shift does not replace its bound builder there.

docs.title: Save to the browser
docs.text: The browser works in both directions: import assets that are already on disk, and save the setups you build in Houdini back into a library. Saved setups rebuild exactly as you left them: parameters, connections, ramps, etc.

docs.title: What you can save
docs.text:
Any network you can select: a Karma / Redshift / Octane material builder, a subnet, a whole material network, or a group of loose nodes. JElib detects the renderer automatically, so there's nothing to tag.

  • Select container nodes (each holding a network) and each is saved as its own asset.
  • Select loose nodes (or a mix) and they're saved together as one asset; they just have to share the same parent network.
  • Select only ramp nodes or Color SOPs and they're saved as a color palette (.ase) rather than a node asset. See Color palettes.

docs.title: Save it
docs.text:
You need two things first: nodes selected in the network editor, and a destination folder selected in the browser's nav tree (it must be one of your own writable libraries; vendor libraries can't be written to).

Then, either:

  • Right-click the node(s) in the network editor → Save Asset [JE], or
  • Drag the selected nodes onto a folder in the browser's nav tree, or onto the grid.
Houdini's node context menu with Save Asset [JE] highlighted at the bottom

JElib asks for a name and saves. The asset appears in the grid under Node Trees, badged with its renderer (KARMA, REDSHIFT, OCTANE, or NODE).

Overwriting an existing asset

Saving under a name that already exists asks first: Overwrite or Cancel. While iterating on the same setup, tick Don't ask again for this asset this session and JElib stops prompting for that asset until you reload the panel. Saving under a new name never prompts.

docs.title: Reuse it
docs.text:
Import a saved setup like any other asset: drag it in, double-click, or Load into Scene. See Import into your scene. JElib rebuilds the network for its renderer.

Use saved setups from sources you trust: loading them or generating thumbnails can run their scripts and expressions. See the saved-network note.

docs.title: Thumbnails for saved assets
docs.text: With Auto-generate on Save enabled (Preferences → Caching), JElib renders a thumbnail for each saved 3D asset automatically. Either way you can right-click the asset → Generate Thumbnail at any time. See Make thumbnails.

docs.title: Working in Solaris (USD)
docs.text: JElib works natively in Solaris. Drop an asset into a LOP network / stage and it builds USD (references, materials, and instancing all native to the stage) instead of the SOP-based setup you'd get in OBJ.

docs.title: It follows your context
docs.text:
Dropping into a Solaris network builds USD automatically: JElib reads the network editor you dropped into, so a multi-asset drop keeps landing in the same stage. Dropping into OBJ builds the classic geo network instead.

Import Into Active Network

The stage is used when Import Into Active Network (Preferences → Import → Advanced) is on. Turn it off to always create a fresh top-level container regardless of where you drop.

docs.title: Bringing geometry into the stage
docs.text:
Models that aren't already USD (see Supported file formats) can enter the stage several ways. Set the default in Preferences → USD → USD Import Mode; override per import in the preview panel's LOP Import:

Mode What lands in the stage Writes to disk? Auto (default) Bakes a .usd sidecar and references it if the asset folder is writable; otherwise falls back to SOP Create Only if writable SOP Create A sopcreate LOP wrapping the import chain No Component Builder A live, editable componentgeometry → componentoutput chain No Bake .usd Always writes <asset>/usd/<name>.usd and references it Yes Use Cached USD References an existing baked .usd as-is; never rebuilds No

The preview panel labels these USD Auto Import · SOP Create · Component Builder · Build USD · Use Cached USD; a rigged/animated FBX swaps the last two build modes for USD Skel and Bake USD. See Animation & sequences.

The baking modes produce a reusable .usd on import. Component Builder keeps the editable network live until you choose Save to Disk on its output node. That export follows your USD cache path and renderer suffix settings, preserves material edits, and becomes available for later cache reuse. SOP Create keeps the import live without writing a cache.

A .usd / .usdc / .usda / .usdz asset needs none of this: it's referenced directly, with no baking and no SOP import. Multi-variant USD plants come in as a single reference with one prim per variant.

docs.title: Reference or sublayer
docs.text:
Preferences → USD → USD Import As controls how the asset composes into the stage:

  • Reference (default) — a reference LOP brings the asset in under its own prim, /<asset_name>. The standard way to bring in a contained asset.
  • Sublayer — a sublayer LOP merges the file's own layer structure into the stage as-is.

docs.title: Baking & reusing caches
docs.text:
When a mode bakes, JElib writes to <asset>/usd/<name>/… next to the source by default. These preferences control the output and cache reuse:

  • Cache to $HIP — write caches under $HIP/usd/… instead, handy when the asset folder is read-only or you'll collect everything with the hip later. (Save your scene first; an unsaved hip falls back to the asset folder with a warning.)
  • Use Baked Cache — when an up-to-date .usd cache already exists, reference it directly instead of rebuilding the Component Builder chain. Much lighter for production scenes.
  • Add Renderer Suffix: on by default, keeps geometry files such as Asset_Karma.usd and Asset_Redshift.usd separate. Turn it off to use Asset.usd; baking with another renderer replaces that shared file. Material-only cache names stay renderer-specific.
  • Clean Up After Bake — after baking, remove the Component Builder nodes and leave just the reference. Re-baking then needs a fresh import.
  • Proxy Detail (%) — how much the Component Builder reduces the proxy representation when baking. It doesn't apply to a $F sequence bake; those author no proxy.

Animated sources bake animated

A $F sequence bakes as a time-sampled USD over its own frame range, not a frozen first frame, and only re-bakes when its frames change. It carries no proxy or collision representation (static assets only). A rigged FBX bakes as a real UsdSkel component, with its own proxy. Either can Loop for the whole scene range. See Animation & sequences.

docs.title: Materials in the stage
docs.text:
JElib builds a materiallibrary and wires a material assignment onto the imported prims for you, with the shader built for your active renderer. Prefer Mtlx Builder changes new Stage materials to USD MaterialX Builders instead. See Renderers & materials for what gets wired.

Viewport preview

Redshift and Octane materials also get a UsdPreviewSurface so they shade in the GL/Storm viewport. Karma and USD MaterialX builders use Houdini's native MaterialX preview behavior.

Select a material builder in its material network and Shift-drag a new material to replace it. Existing Assign Material LOPs follow the replacement. A Scene View drop assigns to the picked object; Shift does not replace its bound builder there.

docs.title: Houdini's native galleries
docs.text:
JElib also registers as a Solaris asset gallery data source, so your libraries appear inside Houdini's own USD tools:

  • Layout Asset Gallery / Stage Manager / Paint Instances — the shared layout gallery defaults to JElib Library on startup and lists your model libraries in their folder hierarchy (vendor libraries group by pack or collection). Rigged/ animated FBX and $F frame sequences appear here alongside static models; VDB and .rs proxy sequences don't, since they import through the volume/proxy LOPs rather than the gallery's model bake.
  • Material Catalog / Material Linker — pick JElib Library from the catalog's source menu to list your materials there.

You can also drag directly from the JElib grid into Stage Manager, Paint Instances or the Material Linker. The drag carries Houdini's own asset payload, so the native tools accept it like one of their items.

Materials dropped this way bake to a small standalone .usd next to the asset (or under $HIP with Cache to $HIP) that references the textures in place: one file per renderer or MaterialX builder choice, using the panel's Material Type. Delete USD Cache in the preview panel removes them. Paths follow Force Absolute File Paths, so gallery references stay portable.

docs.title: Kits & asset packs
docs.text:
A multi-model FBX kit (a full city kit, a props pack) bakes as a USD assembly holding a component per model. What that buys you:

  • A gallery card per model. The Asset Catalog fans the kit out into one card per building; the whole-kit card still drops the city in its authored layout.
  • Light references. Each model writes a small USD of its own beside the pack, so referencing one building from Stage Manager never opens the whole city.
  • Scattering picks models. Create Instances on a kit mixes the kit's models as prototypes (whichever instance method you pick), and a Choose models toggle in the inspector opens a picker for which pieces scatter: leave the dumpsters out.
  • Per-model viewport proxies. Every model carries proxy geometry: dense pieces decimated, small pieces passed through, very heavy pieces (500k+ faces) a bounding box, so a scattered city stays responsive in the viewport.

Kit detection is automatic (all meshes named into groups, 8 or more groups), and the cards get their pictures from the viewport moments after the bake lands.

docs.title: Instancing in the stage
docs.text:
With Create Instances on, a Solaris import builds a native USD PointInstancer rather than the SOP copy-to-points setup used in OBJ. The same distribution and wind controls apply.

Which LOP it lands as depends on the instance method picked in the preview panel, and on your Houdini version:

Method H20.5 / H21 H22 Copy to Points (default) the Instancer LOP the same node, renamed Copy to Points, matching its SOP counterpart Point Instancer (H22) not available the PointInstancer LOP, the same points with the prototypes named outright Scatter Instances (H22) not available the Scatter Instances LOP, which scatters onto a surface and authors the PointInstancer in one node

Same node, new name

H22 renamed the Instancer LOP to Copy to Points; scenes and scripts using the old instancer type still resolve to it. Point Instancer and Scatter Instances are separate, H22-only nodes; the panel greys them out on older builds.

Point Instancer vs. Copy to Points. Both scatter the same points and both land a native USD PointInstancer. The difference is how the prototypes are named: Copy to Points goes through a Collection LOP and a %collection token, while Point Instancer hands the PointInstancer LOP an explicit pattern of the prototype prims. That is what an asset pack or a swapped-in model has to agree with. Nothing else changes, including the timing and distribution controls.

Where the scatter points come from. The instancer always reads its points from a SOP network: reading them from the incoming stage instead gives a shader nothing to vary per copy, so colour, scale and variant stay identical across the scatter. Instance Setup (Preferences → USD) chooses where that network lives:

  • Inside the instancer (default) — one self-contained node. The points never reach the scene graph, so there is no stray geometry to hide.
  • Separate SOP Create node — the same network in a SOP Create node beside the instancer, so you can select and repoint it without diving inside.

docs.title: Per-instance time offset in the stage
docs.text:
An animated asset with Create Instances on gets a Cache LOP + Retime Instances so scattered copies play at different phases. New setups expose the following controls on the retime wrangle inside Retime Instances:

Control What it does Mode Random uses a seed; Step follows instance IDs and a remap ramp; Noise uses frequency, offset, and contrast; Custom reads a named float point attribute. Loop Start Sets the prototype's starting offset. Timing Spread Sets the offset spread in frames. Shared setups scale it by each model's clip length. Defaults to 24. Timing Variants Sets the number of distinct offsets. More variants require more prototypes. Defaults to 24. Stagger Starts Changes how the offsets stagger playback starts. Use Whole Frames Rounds the final offsets to whole frames. On by default.

Step Remap starts as a linear ramp, Noise Frequency defaults to 1, and Custom Attribute defaults to animAttrib. Custom values are clamped to 0-1 and grouped into timing variants. Existing scene nodes keep their current controls; import again to use the new modes. OBJ/SOP controls are described in Per-instance time offset.

Several models can share one instancer. Multi-select two or more Create-Instances models and drop them together. Static models share one scatter; animated models can join with each copy offset within its own asset's clip length. A static model without a cached USD can still join through its selected USD Import mode. Assets that cannot safely join, such as a kit or two assets claiming the same stage prim, keep separate chains, and the footer says why. Single USD Node (Preferences → USD, on by default) lists compatible selected models and plants on one reference or sublayer node, with or without Create Instances. The preview has the same session choice. Live imports, Loop chains, and conflicting USD namespaces keep their own nodes.

.abc sequences stay excluded from Create Instances everywhere; the retiming table gives the reason.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Renderer not installed? The USD geometry still loads; the material is just skipped, so you get untextured geo. Switch to an installed renderer and re-import.
  • Read-only asset folder? Auto quietly falls back to SOP Create (no cache). Use Bake .usd + Cache to $HIP to force a reusable cache elsewhere.
  • Proxy Detail, Component Builder, and material building don't apply to native USD files; those are referenced exactly as authored.

docs.title: Make thumbnails
docs.text: JElib renders thumbnails for your assets (models, materials, HDRIs, and textures) and caches them, so you can read the whole grid at a glance. An asset without one shows a placeholder until you generate it.

docs.title: Generate a thumbnail
docs.text:
Right-click one or more assets in the grid → Generate Thumbnail (or Generate N Thumbnails for a multi-selection). It works for models, materials, saved node trees, HDRIs, textures, and atlases.

A progress dialog shows while it renders. Geometry, HDRI, and texture previews run in the background so the panel stays responsive; material previews render in your live Houdini session.

Saved node networks

Rendering a thumbnail for a saved node network or material rebuilds and evaluates it in Houdini, so its scripts and expressions can run with your user account's permissions. JElib does not sandbox these networks; only load or generate thumbnails for saved setups from sources you trust.

Generate vs cache

Generate Thumbnail renders a new image. The Cache Thumbnails button in Preferences is different: it only pre-scales images you already have for faster display. See The thumbnail cache below.

docs.title: What each thumbnail shows
docs.text:
Asset How it's rendered Model An OpenGL shot of the actual mesh, no shaderball. Material / saved shader The material on a shaderball, lit with studio lights, in your active renderer (default Karma). HDRI The environment map itself, tonemapped. Texture / atlas A 2D preview of the image.

The renderer used for material previews follows the toolbar renderer selector.

For numbered BGEO, compressed BGEO, and Alembic sequences, Generate Thumbnail renders the first frame in the sequence, regardless of its starting number.

docs.title: Auto-generate on save
docs.text: With Auto-generate on Save on (Preferences → Caching, on by default), JElib renders a thumbnail automatically whenever you save a 3D asset into the browser via Save to the browser. It skips assets that already have one, so it never re-renders needlessly. Right-click → Generate Thumbnail always works regardless of this setting.

docs.title: Style the material preview
docs.text:
Preferences → Thumbnail Appearance shapes how material previews look (models, HDRIs, and textures ignore these):

  • Use Simple Sphere — render on a plain sphere instead of the shaderball. Better for tiling materials, where the shaderball's grooves distract.
  • Use HDRI + HDRI Path — light the preview with an environment map instead of the default studio lights. Leave the path empty for the built-in default.

Caption Alignment sets where the name sits under the asset card: Center, Left, or Right.

docs.title: The thumbnail cache
docs.text:
Thumbnails are stored as JPGs under your cache folder (Preferences → Caching → Thumbnail Cache, $JE_ASSET_BROWSER_CACHE). Two buttons manage the cache:

  • Cache Thumbnails — pre-scale every existing preview into the cache for fast grid display. This does not render new thumbnails.
  • Clear Cache — delete pre-scaled thumbnails and every generated geometry, material, HDRI, and texture preview. Original asset and vendor preview files are kept.

JElib also caches quietly in the background as you browse, so the grid fills in on its own.

docs.title: Manage a thumbnail
docs.text:
Right-click an asset:

  • Set Thumbnail… — pick your own image file to use as the asset's thumbnail, replacing the rendered one.
  • Open Thumbnail Folder — reveal the cached image in Explorer/Finder.
  • Delete Thumbnail: remove the generated or custom image. The card shows an available baked USD preview, or a placeholder if none exists.

After a model USD bake, its preview appears in the grid and inspector without a library rescan. Custom, generated, and vendor previews take priority over the bake's thumbnail.

docs.title: Collect Files
docs.text:
Collect Files gathers supported scene dependencies, including textures, HDRIs, caches, and files referenced inside USD layers. It copies the selected files into one folder together with a copy of your hip file. A complete collection is ready for handoff, archive, or another machine. A partial collection also saves the scene copy and reports inputs that still use external files. Your current scene stays open, with its original paths restored.

Relink Files repairs broken paths in the working scene. Collect copies the dependencies and saves a portable scene alongside them.

Open it from JElib → Collect Files… in Houdini's main menu.

Free edition

In the Free edition this menu entry reads Collect Files (Paid)… and opens the purchase prompt.

docs.title: 1. Choose a target folder
docs.text: At the top, Target is where everything gets copied; it defaults to $HIP/collects. Type a path or click Browse…. Editing it (or clicking Rescan) re-scans the scene.

docs.title: 2. Review what will be collected
docs.text:
Dependencies are grouped into a tree by where they'll land, with four columns:

Column Shows Destination the sub-folder each file goes to (with a checkbox; see below) Category its type (textures, geo, a whole vendor asset…) Size file/asset size Status ok, missing, cloud (online-only), or in_target (already there)

Include or exclude with the checkbox on each row; only green ok files can be collected. Render inputs start unchecked. Missing or unchecked inputs remain external and are listed in the collection report. For a loose image, a small dropdown lets you reclassify it between tex and render if it landed in the wrong bucket.

The running total above the buttons shows files · assets · size so you know how big the collect will be before you start.

docs.title: 3. Collect
docs.text:
• Collect copies the ticked files into <target>/<hipname>/ and saves a <hipname>.hip inside it. Collected files use $HIP-relative paths, so a complete collection works wherever you move it.
  • Collect + Zip stages the selected files and scene copy, then saves a single <hipname>.zip. A successful collection leaves only the archive; existing files in the chosen destination stay in place.

The confirmation separates the file count, destination and action. Progress labels distinguish copying, saving and archiving. You can cancel mid-collect; files already copied remain available for recovery. A failed archive build keeps the previous archive.

Either way your session stays on your original file. A plain Collect ends with a saved scene copy. Click Open Scene Copy to open it, or Done to finish (the collected folder is revealed in your file manager). Collect + Zip reveals the finished zip instead. Review Details opens diagnostics without closing the result. Partial collections record external inputs in collection_report.json, inside the collected folder or archive.

Review those external inputs before handing off a partial collection. A report that cannot be written leaves the saved scene copy in place and prevents zip creation.

docs.title: What it collects
docs.text:
Collect follows the same references as Relink (file parameters and any string parm pointing at a known media/geo file) and is smart about grouping:

  • Whole vendor assets. A non-USD file inside a Greyscalegorilla / Quixel / Fab asset brings the entire asset folder along, structure intact, not just the one map. PBR sets and model+texture bundles are copied whole too.
  • Sequences & UDIMs. $F frame sequences and <UDIM> tiles are gathered as a complete set, with the token preserved in the repathed value.
  • USD layers. Referenced .usd, .usda, and .usdc files bring their nested sublayers, references, payloads, textures, and other authored file dependencies. USD value clips follow their authored timing settings. USD copies use relative paths within their own collected folder; source layers stay unchanged. This also applies to USD roots inside vendor asset folders.
  • Substance archives. A material imported from an .sbsar brings its baked maps, so the collected scene renders without the archive. An archive that a Substance node points at is collected with the textures.
  • Name collisions are handled automatically: a colliding file gets a _1, _2… suffix so nothing overwrites.

Like Relink, it skips output paths, tool executables, temp files and inactive built-in references. Supported expressions are evaluated in context. Active File Cache disk inputs remain available for collection.

These are reported as external inputs in a partial collection:

  • Missing files
  • Online-only files (download them first)
  • Excluded dependencies
  • Copy or path errors

These are unsupported and remain external in the saved scene copy: USD packages (.usdz), folder references, and dependencies that don't resolve to local files.

USD clip templates require their path, start, end, and stride in the same metadata block. Timing settings split across layers are unsupported.

docs.title: Relink Files
docs.text:
Relink Files finds supported file references in your scene, flags the ones whose files are missing, and lets you repoint them at files that already exist on disk. Ordinary file repairs update node parameters. Repairs inside USD layers create scene-local USD copies and repoint the owning nodes to them. Use Collect Files to gather the whole scene's dependencies.

Open it from JElib → Relink Files… in Houdini's main menu.

Free edition

In the Free edition this menu entry reads Relink Files (Paid)… and opens the purchase prompt.

docs.title: The window
docs.text:
The dialog scans your scene the moment it opens and lists references in a table:

Column Shows Node the node holding the reference (double-click to jump to it) Parameter the parameter name, plus the source layer for a path inside USD Path the file path (double-click to edit inline) Status Missing, OK, or → Pending (a staged change)

Missing references sort to the top. Missing only (on by default) hides the healthy ones; the Filter… field narrows the list live.

Healthy inputs use the green OK status. Messages, progress windows and choices open as children of the Relink window, with an emphasized primary action.

docs.title: Fix broken paths
docs.text:
Nothing is written until you Commit: every action below just stages a proposal, turning the row → Pending. That's your safety net: stage freely, review, then commit (it's a single undo, too).

USD repairs create copies in $HIP/usd/relinked; source layers stay unchanged. Save the scene before committing an internal USD repair. Undo restores the node paths, while the generated copies remain on disk.

  • Relink by Folder… — the fast path. Pick a New Root Folder and JElib searches it (recursively, case-insensitive) for files matching the missing names and stages the matches. Two fallbacks kick in for names that don't match exactly:
    • Other resolutions — if a texture no longer exists at its referenced resolution (a re-downloaded pack now shipping _4K_ where the scene expects _8K_), a popup lists the resolutions that do exist, largest first with counts. One pick stages every reference available at that resolution; the rest stay Missing, so re-run for stragglers.
    • GSG catalog renames — GSG files that were renamed across catalog re-releases (GSG_Terrazzo_34A_basecolor → GSG_MC010_A067_Terrazzo34A_4k_basecolor) are recovered by fuzzy matching: the texture channel must match exactly and only a clearly-best candidate is proposed (ambiguous cases stay Missing). These stage as → Pending (fuzzy 79%) — review the proposed paths before you Commit.
  • Find → replace + Apply — string-swap part of every path, e.g. $OLD_ROOT → $JOB. Works on selected rows, or all of them if none are selected.
  • Right-click a row → Browse for File… — pick a replacement by hand.
  • Use Relative Path / right-click Relativize Path — convert absolute paths to $ENV-relative where possible, for portability.

When you're happy, click Commit to write all staged paths at once. The status line reports what happened, e.g. Committed 12 path(s). (0 missing / 47 total). Closing the window with staged-but-uncommitted paths asks first (Commit and Close, Discard and Close, or Cancel), so staged work is never dropped silently.

Export a missing list

Export Missing… writes a text list of every unresolved reference, handy for chasing down files or handing the list to whoever has them.

docs.title: What it scans
docs.text:
Relink looks at Houdini's own file references plus any string parameter pointing at a known media or geo file (.exr, .tx, .abc, .usd, .fbx, and so on). It's token-aware: $F frame sequences and <UDIM> tiles are matched as a set, and a committed relink keeps the token in the parameter rather than pinning it to one file. Expression-driven paths (backtick chs(...) references and the like) are evaluated in context, so they show their real status, and relinking one preserves the expression.

For .usd, .usda, and .usdc roots, it also checks files authored inside nested sublayers, references, payloads, and asset-valued attributes, including textures and value-clip templates. The table keeps the owning Houdini node and identifies the source USD layer. Replacing a USD root rescans its dependencies so newly exposed missing files can be repaired too.

Internal repairs require all dependencies of the repaired USD root to be available as local files. Internal repairs for USD file sequences are unsupported; relinking the sequence's node path still preserves its frame token. USD packages (.usdz), folder references, and paths that don't resolve to local files are unsupported and reported. Download online-only files before repairing their USD references.

USD clip templates require their path, start, end, and stride in the same metadata block. Timing settings split across layers are unsupported. Folder relinking keeps the template's hash tokens; a single numbered frame cannot replace a template.

It skips output paths, tool executables, inactive built-in references and Houdini temp files, which aren't broken input references. Windows paths beginning with a slash are recognized as rooted paths.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Quick fixes for the snags you're most likely to hit.

docs.title: The Browse grid is empty
docs.text: JElib isn't pointed at any assets yet. Add a library. See Adding your libraries.

docs.title: My asset imported but has no material / renders untextured
docs.text: The material's renderer isn't loaded. JElib skips the material and still loads the geometry when the chosen renderer's plugin is missing. Switch the toolbar renderer to one you have installed and re-import. See Renderers & materials.

docs.title: A Substance archive won't load
docs.text: JElib's import note names the reason. "this Houdini version can't read Substance archives" means this Houdini build is missing the Substance node JElib bakes with, so import the archive in another Houdini version. "the Substance archive couldn't be read" means the file is damaged or isn't a valid archive, so download it again. See Substance archives.

docs.title: Dragging a file from Explorer/Finder does nothing
docs.text: External drops need all three: the panel open (and visible, not behind another tab), the drop over the network editor, and Handle External File Drops on (Preferences → Import → Advanced). They don't work in the viewport or on parameter fields. See Import into your scene.

docs.title: My atlas scattered as one big grid
docs.text: The Atlas Splitter HDA isn't installed, so the atlas loaded onto a flat grid with no piece splitting. Install the HDA to trace the packed cards. See Texture atlases.

docs.title: An asset shows an exclamation mark and won't load
docs.text: It lives on a remote/NAS source that's currently unreachable. Reconnect (check the NAS / Tailscale connection) and try again. See Remote & cloud libraries.

docs.title: New files I added to the NAS or a cloud folder aren't showing
docs.text:
A plain Reload re-checks every NAS / on-demand library by default (the accurate-but-slower option), so files you added or removed normally appear right away. If they don't, that library has Trust Cache on Reload on: turn it off in the nav tree's right-click menu, or Shift-/Ctrl-click Reload to force a full re-walk. For just one library, right-click it → Reload This Library.

Cloud-sync libraries (Dropbox / Google Drive / OneDrive / iCloud Drive / Synology Drive) auto-detect changes on every reload by default. If new files aren't showing, check whether Preferences → Caching → Trust Cloud Library Cache Without Verifying is turned on. If so, that library behaves like the NAS case above and needs the same Shift/Ctrl-click or per-library force-reload.

docs.title: Thumbnails aren't appearing
docs.text: Cache Thumbnails only pre-scales previews that already exist; it doesn't render new ones. To generate missing thumbnails, right-click assets → Generate Thumbnail. See Make thumbnails.

docs.title: A scene's file paths are broken
docs.text: Use Relink Files to repoint references at where the files actually are.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Inside Houdini: JElib → Check for Updates… When a newer release exists:

  • Free edition — choose Download & Install. JElib downloads the new version to your Downloads folder and updates itself in place. If that button isn't offered, use Open Download Page like the Paid edition.
  • Paid edition — choose Open Download Page, save the zip, then choose Install Downloaded Zip… and pick it.

A confirmation shows what will change, then JElib asks you to restart Houdini. Your libraries, favorites, and cache are all kept. Install Downloaded Zip… also installs an older zip if you ever need to roll back.

docs.title: Running the installer instead
docs.text:
Unzip the new version and run Install_JElib_Windows.bat / Install_JElib_macOS.command (or "<Houdini>/bin/hython" setup_jelib.py) exactly like a first install.

It detects your existing install and asks a single "Upgrade vX → vY in place?" On Yes it updates the code where it already lives and refreshes the package config without re-asking where anything goes.

Free updates and edition changes

Use the downloaded version's installer when updating Free or switching between Free and Paid. It removes files left by the previous version while keeping your libraries, favorites, and cache.
